description: Class-level drug interaction rules. Each rule names drug classes (or single ingredients), a grade on the site's A-E scale, the syndrome, a plain-language mechanism and action, the TEST_PACK.md rulebook row it implements, and its sources. Members are lowercase RxNorm base ingredient names; a member also matches a longer base name that starts with it and a space (lithium matches lithium carbonate). Grades: E do not use together; D avoid or change therapy; C monitor closely or adjust; B monitor; A minor.

seizure_lowering.plural: drugs that lower the seizure threshold

polyvalent_cation.plural: calcium, iron, magnesium, aluminum, or zinc products

levothyroxine_binder.plural: drugs that bind levothyroxine in the gut

groups.risk: risk of oversedation, slowed breathing (respiratory depression), falls, and overdose
groups.mechanism: Each drug depresses the brain on its own; together the effects add up. Opioids with benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids, or other sedatives can stop breathing: both opioid and benzodiazepine labels carry a boxed warning on this combination.
groups.action: Use the lowest doses for the shortest time, avoid adding more sedatives, and watch for sleepiness and slow or shallow breathing. With an opioid, co-prescribe naloxone.

groups.mechanism: Each drug raises serotonin activity. Together they can cause serotonin syndrome: agitation, tremor, clonus and overactive reflexes, sweating, fever, fast heart rate.
groups.action: Avoid stacking serotonergic drugs where possible; if needed, use low doses and watch for clonus, tremor, fever, and agitation, especially in the first days after a start or dose increase.

groups.risk: risk of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes
groups.mechanism: Each drug slows the heart's electrical recovery (the QT interval). Together the effect adds up and can trigger torsades de pointes, a dangerous heart rhythm.
groups.action: Get a baseline ECG and keep potassium and magnesium normal. Stop or switch a drug if the QTc passes 500 ms.

groups.risk: low potassium and magnesium from the diuretic raise the rhythm risk
groups.mechanism: Loop and thiazide diuretics lower potassium and magnesium. Low levels make QT-prolonging drugs more likely to cause torsades and make digoxin more toxic.
groups.action: Check potassium and magnesium at the start and after dose changes; replace them to keep potassium above 4.0 mmol/L.

groups.risk: risk of serious bleeding, especially stomach and gut bleeding
groups.mechanism: Anticoagulants slow clotting, aspirin and other antiplatelets stop platelets from sticking, NSAIDs block platelets and injure the stomach lining, and SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need. Each added drug raises the bleeding risk.
groups.action: Drop any drug that is not essential (WOEST and AUGUSTUS support dropping aspirin from triple therapy), add a proton pump inhibitor for stomach protection, and watch for black stools, vomiting blood, or anemia.

groups.mechanism: ACE inhibitors and ARBs lower aldosterone, spironolactone and eplerenone block it, trimethoprim blocks the kidney's potassium channel (like amiloride), and supplements add potassium. Together potassium can rise to levels that stop the heart.
groups.action: Check potassium and kidney function within 3 days and again at 1 week; stop the potassium supplement or change the antibiotic when possible.

groups.mechanism: NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that keep blood flowing into the kidney, ACE inhibitors and ARBs lower the pressure that keeps it filtering, and diuretics reduce blood volume (the "triple whammy"). Aminoglycosides, vancomycin, and other listed drugs injure the kidney directly.
groups.action: Avoid the NSAID if possible, keep the patient hydrated, and check creatinine within a week, sooner in the hospital.

groups.risk: risk of low blood pressure on standing, fainting, and falls
groups.mechanism: Each drug lowers blood pressure or blocks the reflex that holds it up when standing. Together they can cause orthostatic hypotension, fainting, and falls.
groups.action: Start low, raise one drug at a time, check standing blood pressure, and tell the patient to stand up slowly.

groups.risk: risk of slow heart rate (bradycardia) and heart block
groups.mechanism: Each drug slows the heart rate or conduction through the AV node. Together they can cause severe bradycardia, AV block, or heart failure.
groups.action: Check pulse and an ECG after starting or raising any of them; lower doses or stop one if the heart rate drops below 50 or new AV block appears.

groups.mechanism: Insulin and sulfonylureas lower glucose regardless of the level; adding more glucose-lowering drugs stacks the effect. Fluoroquinolones carry a label warning for severe blood-sugar swings, and beta-blockers hide the shaking and fast heartbeat that warn of a low.
groups.action: Lower the insulin or sulfonylurea dose when adding another agent, check glucose more often, and teach the patient to recognize lows without the usual warning signs.

groups.risk: anticholinergic burden: confusion, urinary retention, constipation, falls
groups.mechanism: Each drug blocks acetylcholine. Together they cause confusion or delirium, dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation or ileus, overheating, and falls, worst in older adults (Beers criteria).
groups.action: Replace the strongest anticholinergic with an alternative and avoid the combination in older adults.

groups.risk: the anticholinergics work against the dementia drug
groups.mechanism: Cholinesterase inhibitors raise acetylcholine to help memory; anticholinergic drugs block acetylcholine. The two work in opposite directions (therapeutic antagonism), so the dementia drug does less and confusion gets worse.
groups.action: Stop or replace the anticholinergic drugs, or reconsider the cholinesterase inhibitor.

groups.mechanism: Tramadol and bupropion lower the seizure threshold in a dose-related way. The other drugs listed lower it too, so the risk adds up.
groups.action: Keep tramadol and bupropion at or below labeled doses, avoid them in patients with seizure risk factors, and prefer alternatives when several threshold-lowering drugs are needed.

groups.mechanism: Thiazides make the kidney lose sodium; SSRIs, SNRIs, carbamazepine, and oxcarbazepine cause the body to hold water (an SIADH-like effect). Together sodium can fall enough to cause confusion, falls, or seizures, most often in older women.
groups.action: Check sodium at baseline and within 2 weeks; choose a non-thiazide diuretic if sodium falls.

pairs.risk: can cause fatal serotonin syndrome
pairs.mechanism: An MAO inhibitor stops the breakdown of serotonin; these drugs release it or block its reuptake. Together serotonin can rise to toxic levels: high fever, rigidity, seizures, death.
pairs.action: Do not use together. Allow the washout the labels require (usually 14 days after stopping an MAO inhibitor, 5 weeks after fluoxetine).

pairs.risk: risk of serotonin syndrome
pairs.mechanism: An MAO inhibitor stops the breakdown of serotonin, and these drugs add serotonin activity. The labels advise against the combination.
pairs.action: Avoid; if unavoidable, start low and monitor closely for agitation, clonus, and fever.

pairs.risk: risk of a hypertensive crisis
pairs.mechanism: Bupropion raises norepinephrine and dopamine; with an MAO inhibitor these build up and can cause a sudden, severe rise in blood pressure. The bupropion label contraindicates the combination and requires 14 days between them.
pairs.action: Do not use together. Wait at least 14 days after stopping the MAO inhibitor.

pairs.risk: risk of a hypertensive crisis
pairs.mechanism: MAO inhibitors stop the breakdown of norepinephrine; stimulants and decongestants release it. Together blood pressure can spike to a hypertensive crisis with stroke or heart damage.
pairs.action: Do not use together, or within 14 days of stopping the MAO inhibitor.

pairs.risk: can cause serotonin syndrome
pairs.mechanism: The rasagiline and selegiline labels contraindicate meperidine, tramadol, methadone, dextromethorphan, and similar drugs because serious, sometimes fatal serotonin syndrome has occurred.
pairs.action: Do not use together; wait at least 14 days after stopping the MAO-B inhibitor.

pairs.risk: boxed warning: profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death
pairs.mechanism: Opioids and benzodiazepines both suppress the brainstem's drive to breathe. Both drug classes carry an FDA boxed warning against this combination.
pairs.action: Avoid when possible. If both are needed, use the lowest doses, limit the duration, co-prescribe naloxone, and monitor breathing and sedation.

pairs.risk: risk of respiratory depression
pairs.mechanism: Gabapentin and pregabalin add to opioid respiratory depression; the FDA added this warning to both in 2019. Both are cleared by the kidney, so kidney injury raises exposure.
pairs.action: Start the gabapentinoid low, adjust for kidney function, and monitor for sedation and slow breathing.

pairs.risk: collapse, respiratory arrest, and cardiac arrest have been reported
pairs.mechanism: The clozapine label warns of collapse, respiratory arrest, and cardiac arrest with benzodiazepines and other psychotropic drugs, especially early in treatment.
pairs.action: Use caution, especially when starting clozapine; monitor breathing and blood pressure.

pairs.risk: the antagonist blocks the opioid and can bring on withdrawal
pairs.mechanism: Naltrexone occupies opioid receptors: it blocks the opioid's effect and precipitates acute withdrawal in a patient who depends on the opioid. The naltrexone label contraindicates use in patients taking opioids. One of these prescriptions is likely an error.
pairs.action: Do not use together. Decide which treatment is intended; naltrexone needs 7 to 10 opioid-free days first.

pairs.risk: opioid levels rise: risk of fatal respiratory depression
pairs.mechanism: These opioids are cleared by CYP3A4. A CYP3A4 inhibitor raises opioid levels (fentanyl and oxycodone roughly 2 to 3 times), and the effect can build over days. The opioid labels carry a boxed warning on CYP3A4 inhibitors.
pairs.action: Avoid if possible; otherwise lower the opioid dose, monitor closely for sedation and slow breathing, and re-adjust when the inhibitor stops.

pairs.risk: statin levels rise many-fold: risk of rhabdomyolysis
pairs.b_plural: drugs the statin label rules out
pairs.mechanism: Simvastatin and lovastatin are cleared almost entirely by CYP3A4. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (and erythromycin, cyclosporine, gemfibrozil, danazol) raise their levels roughly 10-fold, causing muscle breakdown and kidney failure. The simvastatin label contraindicates these combinations.
pairs.action: Do not use together. Hold the statin during the antibiotic or antifungal course, or switch to pravastatin or rosuvastatin.

pairs.risk: raises the statin level: risk of muscle injury
pairs.b_plural: drugs that raise the statin level
pairs.mechanism: These drugs slow simvastatin's clearance. The simvastatin label caps the dose at 10 mg a day with verapamil, diltiazem, or dronedarone, and 20 mg with amiodarone, amlodipine, or ranolazine.
pairs.action: Keep simvastatin at or below the label's cap, or switch to a statin not cleared by CYP3A4 (pravastatin, rosuvastatin).

pairs.risk: atorvastatin levels rise: risk of muscle injury
pairs.b_plural: drugs that raise the atorvastatin level
pairs.mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors raise atorvastatin exposure several-fold. The atorvastatin label limits the dose (20 mg with clarithromycin, itraconazole, or boosted protease inhibitors) and advises avoiding cyclosporine, gemfibrozil, and tipranavir.
pairs.action: Use the lowest atorvastatin dose (at most 20 mg with these), or switch to pravastatin or rosuvastatin; watch for muscle pain and dark urine.

pairs.risk: risk of rhabdomyolysis
pairs.mechanism: Gemfibrozil blocks statin uptake into the liver (OATP1B1) and its glucuronidation, raising statin levels, and adds its own muscle toxicity.
pairs.action: Avoid; use fenofibrate if a fibrate is needed.

pairs.risk: colchicine levels rise: risk of fatal colchicine toxicity
pairs.b_plural: drugs that block CYP3A4 or P-glycoprotein
pairs.mechanism: Colchicine is cleared by CYP3A4 and pumped out by P-glycoprotein (P-gp). Blocking these raises colchicine to toxic levels (diarrhea, muscle damage, bone-marrow failure); fatal cases are reported. The colchicine label contraindicates these inhibitors in patients with kidney or liver impairment and requires a lower dose otherwise.
pairs.action: Reduce the colchicine dose as the label directs (for gout prophylaxis, 0.3 mg a day or less) or avoid; do not combine at all with kidney or liver impairment.

pairs.risk: colchicine levels rise
pairs.mechanism: Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (and the weak P-glycoprotein effect of diltiazem) raise colchicine levels. The colchicine label calls for a dose reduction.
pairs.action: Lower the colchicine dose as the label directs and watch for diarrhea, muscle pain, and low blood counts.

pairs.risk: additive muscle toxicity
pairs.mechanism: Colchicine and statins can each injure muscle; myopathy and rhabdomyolysis have been reported with the combination, worse when a CYP3A4 inhibitor raises both.
pairs.action: Watch for muscle pain or weakness and check CK if symptoms appear.

pairs.risk: sedative levels rise many-fold: prolonged, deep sedation
pairs.mechanism: Triazolam and oral midazolam depend on CYP3A4; ketoconazole raises triazolam exposure more than 20-fold. The labels contraindicate strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.
pairs.action: Do not use together; choose a benzodiazepine not cleared by CYP3A4 (lorazepam, temazepam) if one is needed.

pairs.risk: alprazolam levels rise: prolonged sedation
pairs.mechanism: Ketoconazole raises alprazolam exposure about 4-fold. The alprazolam label contraindicates ketoconazole and itraconazole.
pairs.action: Do not use together; use lorazepam or another benzodiazepine not cleared by CYP3A4.

pairs.risk: alprazolam levels rise: prolonged sedation and slowed breathing
pairs.mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ritonavir, cobicistat, and clarithromycin raise alprazolam exposure; the label advises avoiding them or cutting the dose.
pairs.action: Avoid, or reduce the alprazolam dose and monitor sedation; lorazepam is an alternative.

pairs.risk: sedative levels rise
pairs.mechanism: Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors raise the levels of benzodiazepines cleared by CYP3A4.
pairs.action: Use a lower benzodiazepine dose and watch for excess sedation.

pairs.risk: lurasidone levels rise many-fold
pairs.mechanism: Ketoconazole raised lurasidone exposure about 9-fold; the lurasidone label contraindicates strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.
pairs.action: Do not use together.

pairs.risk: lurasidone levels fall about 80%: it stops working
pairs.mechanism: Rifampin cut lurasidone exposure by about 80%; the lurasidone label contraindicates strong CYP3A4 inducers because the drug loses its effect (efficacy loss).
pairs.action: Do not use together; choose an antipsychotic less dependent on CYP3A4.

pairs.risk: quetiapine levels rise about 6-fold
pairs.mechanism: Ketoconazole raised quetiapine exposure about 6-fold; the quetiapine label says to cut the dose to one-sixth with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.
pairs.action: Reduce quetiapine to one-sixth of the dose, or avoid.

pairs.risk: quetiapine levels rise
pairs.mechanism: Quetiapine is cleared by CYP3A4; moderate inhibitors raise its level, adding sedation, low blood pressure, and QT effect.
pairs.action: Watch for sedation and dizziness; lower the quetiapine dose if they appear.

pairs.risk: haloperidol levels rise: more QT and movement side effects
pairs.mechanism: Haloperidol is partly cleared by CYP3A4; inhibitors raise its level, adding QT prolongation and extrapyramidal side effects.
pairs.action: Monitor for stiffness, restlessness, and QT changes; lower the dose if needed.

pairs.risk: immunosuppressant levels rise: kidney and nerve toxicity
pairs.mechanism: Tacrolimus and cyclosporine are narrow-margin drugs cleared by CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein. Azoles, macrolides, diltiazem, and verapamil raise their levels, causing kidney injury, tremor and seizures, high potassium, and high blood pressure.
pairs.action: Reduce the immunosuppressant dose pre-emptively and check trough levels within a few days of starting or stopping the inhibitor.

pairs.risk: immunosuppressant levels fall: risk of rejection
pairs.mechanism: Enzyme inducers speed tacrolimus and cyclosporine clearance, so levels fall sharply within 1 to 2 weeks (efficacy loss) and graft rejection can follow.
pairs.action: Avoid if possible; otherwise raise the dose and follow trough levels closely, including after the inducer stops.

pairs.risk: tacrolimus levels may rise slightly
pairs.mechanism: Omeprazole and lansoprazole weakly inhibit CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 and can modestly raise tacrolimus levels, mainly in CYP2C19 poor metabolizers.
pairs.action: Usually no change; check a tacrolimus level if one is due.

pairs.risk: anticoagulant levels rise: risk of major bleeding
pairs.b_plural: drugs that block CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein
pairs.mechanism: These drugs block both CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, the two routes that clear apixaban and rivaroxaban, roughly doubling their levels.
pairs.action: Avoid, or use the reduced dose the label specifies (apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily), and watch closely for bleeding.

pairs.risk: dabigatran levels rise: risk of major bleeding
pairs.mechanism: Dabigatran is moved out of the gut by P-glycoprotein (P-gp) and cleared about 80% by the kidney. Dronedarone and ketoconazole block P-gp and roughly double dabigatran exposure.
pairs.action: Avoid when kidney function is reduced (CrCl below 50 mL/min); otherwise follow the label's dose reduction and watch for bleeding.

pairs.risk: dabigatran levels rise
pairs.mechanism: These drugs block P-glycoprotein (P-gp) and raise dabigatran levels; verapamil raises them 50 to 180% depending on timing.
pairs.action: Give dabigatran at least 2 hours before verapamil, check kidney function, and watch for bleeding.

pairs.risk: anticoagulant levels fall: risk of stroke or clot
pairs.mechanism: Rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, and St. John's wort induce CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein and roughly halve DOAC exposure, so the anticoagulant can fail (efficacy loss).
pairs.action: Avoid; use another anticoagulant (such as warfarin with INR monitoring) while the inducer is needed.

pairs.risk: INR rises: risk of serious bleeding
pairs.mechanism: These drugs block CYP2C9, which clears S-warfarin (the more potent half of warfarin). The INR can double within days; amiodarone's effect lasts for weeks after it stops.
pairs.action: Choose another drug if possible; otherwise lower the warfarin dose (often 25 to 50%) and check the INR within 3 to 5 days.

pairs.risk: INR swings both ways: bleeding risk first, then clotting risk; phenytoin levels may rise
pairs.mechanism: Phenytoin first displaces warfarin from albumin and raises the INR (bleeding risk), then induces its metabolism and lowers the INR (clot risk); warfarin can also raise phenytoin levels.
pairs.action: Check the INR and phenytoin levels often when either drug is started, stopped, or changed.

pairs.risk: INR falls: risk of clots
pairs.mechanism: These drugs induce CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 and speed warfarin clearance, so the INR falls over 1 to 2 weeks.
pairs.action: Check the INR weekly and raise the warfarin dose as needed; lower it again after the inducer stops.

pairs.risk: phenytoin levels rise: toxicity (unsteadiness, confusion)
pairs.mechanism: Phenytoin is cleared by CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 with saturable kinetics, so a small drop in clearance causes a large rise in level. These drugs inhibit those enzymes.
pairs.action: Check a phenytoin level within 1 to 2 weeks and watch for nystagmus, unsteadiness, and confusion.

pairs.risk: sulfonylurea levels rise: severe, prolonged low blood sugar
pairs.mechanism: These drugs block CYP2C9 (or CYP3A4), which clears sulfonylureas, so the sulfonylurea accumulates. Severe hypoglycemia lasting more than a day is reported, especially in older adults.
pairs.action: Choose another antibiotic if possible, or lower the sulfonylurea dose and check glucose often during the course.

pairs.risk: slow heart rate, and a rebound hypertensive crisis if clonidine stops suddenly
pairs.mechanism: Both slow the heart. If clonidine is stopped abruptly, norepinephrine surges; with alpha receptors unopposed under beta-blockade, blood pressure can rebound to a crisis.
pairs.action: Monitor heart rate. To stop, taper the beta-blocker first and then clonidine over several days.

pairs.risk: severe bradycardia, heart block, heart failure
pairs.mechanism: Beta-blockers and verapamil or diltiazem both slow the AV node and weaken heart contraction. Together they can cause profound bradycardia, AV block, or cardiogenic shock.
pairs.action: Avoid unless monitored; check pulse and ECG, and avoid in heart failure or conduction disease.

pairs.risk: digoxin levels rise: toxicity
pairs.mechanism: These drugs block P-glycoprotein, the pump that clears digoxin, and raise digoxin levels by 50 to 150% (amiodarone about 70%, dronedarone about 2.5-fold). Digoxin has a narrow margin.
pairs.action: Halve the digoxin dose when starting amiodarone or dronedarone, and check a digoxin level within 1 to 2 weeks (target 0.5 to 0.9 ng/mL in heart failure).

pairs.risk: digoxin levels rise
pairs.mechanism: Verapamil raises digoxin 50 to 75% and diltiazem 20 to 50% by blocking P-glycoprotein, and both add to digoxin's slowing of the heart.
pairs.action: Check a digoxin level and heart rate after starting; lower the digoxin dose if needed.

pairs.risk: lithium levels rise: lithium toxicity
pairs.mechanism: The kidney handles lithium like sodium. Thiazides (levels up 25 to 40%), ACE inhibitors and ARBs, and NSAIDs all make the kidney hold on to lithium. Toxicity brings coarse tremor, unsteadiness, confusion, and arrhythmia.
pairs.action: Avoid if possible; otherwise lower the lithium dose and check a lithium level within 5 to 7 days (therapeutic range 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L), plus kidney function and sodium.

pairs.risk: lithium levels may rise
pairs.b_plural: drugs that can raise lithium levels
pairs.mechanism: Volume loss and reduced kidney clearance can raise lithium levels.
pairs.action: Check a lithium level after starting and watch for tremor or confusion.

pairs.risk: bone-marrow suppression, even at low weekly doses
pairs.mechanism: Trimethoprim blocks the same folate enzyme (DHFR) as methotrexate, and sulfamethoxazole reduces methotrexate's kidney clearance. Fatal pancytopenia is reported even with low weekly methotrexate.
pairs.action: Avoid; choose another antibiotic. If unavoidable, check blood counts and consider leucovorin.

pairs.risk: methotrexate clearance falls: kidney and marrow toxicity
pairs.mechanism: NSAIDs reduce the kidney's secretion of methotrexate (OAT1 and OAT3) and can lower kidney function, raising methotrexate levels. The risk is highest with high methotrexate doses.
pairs.action: Monitor blood counts, kidney function, and liver tests; avoid NSAIDs around high-dose methotrexate.

pairs.risk: methotrexate clearance falls
pairs.mechanism: Penicillins compete with methotrexate for kidney secretion and can raise its levels.
pairs.action: Monitor blood counts and watch for mouth sores.

pairs.risk: methotrexate clearance may fall
pairs.mechanism: Proton pump inhibitors can slow methotrexate elimination, mainly with high-dose methotrexate.
pairs.action: Consider holding the proton pump inhibitor around high-dose methotrexate.

pairs.risk: additive bone-marrow suppression
pairs.mechanism: Both drugs suppress the bone marrow; the effects add.
pairs.action: Check blood counts regularly.

pairs.risk: thiopurine levels rise: severe bone marrow suppression (myelosuppression)
pairs.mechanism: Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase, a main route for clearing 6-mercaptopurine (azathioprine's active form), shunting it to toxic thioguanine nucleotides.
pairs.action: Reduce azathioprine or mercaptopurine to one-third to one-quarter of the dose, or avoid; check blood counts often.

pairs.risk: severe bone-marrow suppression
pairs.mechanism: Febuxostat blocks xanthine oxidase; its label contraindicates azathioprine and mercaptopurine.
pairs.action: Do not use together.

pairs.risk: agranulocytosis risk adds up, and clozapine levels fall
pairs.mechanism: Both drugs can cause agranulocytosis, and carbamazepine induces CYP3A4 and roughly halves clozapine levels.
pairs.action: Avoid; choose another mood stabilizer.

pairs.risk: tamoxifen may not work
pairs.mechanism: Tamoxifen works through its active metabolite endoxifen, made by CYP2D6. Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors cut endoxifen levels, which has been associated with more breast cancer recurrence (efficacy loss).
pairs.action: Avoid; for depression choose an antidepressant with little CYP2D6 effect (venlafaxine, escitalopram, citalopram).

pairs.risk: tricyclic levels rise: toxicity, QT prolongation, seizures
pairs.mechanism: Tricyclics are cleared by CYP2D6. Strong inhibitors can raise tricyclic levels several-fold, causing anticholinergic toxicity, QT prolongation, and seizures.
pairs.action: Use a low tricyclic dose and check a level, or choose another drug.

pairs.risk: atomoxetine levels rise 6- to 8-fold
pairs.mechanism: Atomoxetine is cleared by CYP2D6. Strong inhibitors raise exposure 6- to 8-fold, like a poor metabolizer: faster heart rate, higher blood pressure, side effects.
pairs.action: Start atomoxetine at 40 mg a day and raise to 80 mg only after 4 weeks if needed, as the label directs.

pairs.risk: less pain relief; more parent-drug side effects
pairs.mechanism: CYP2D6 turns codeine into morphine and tramadol into its active opioid metabolite. Blocking it reduces pain relief, and for tramadol leaves more parent drug with its seizure and serotonin effects.
pairs.action: Expect weaker analgesia; watch for serotonin effects with tramadol, and consider a different analgesic.

pairs.risk: may change the opioid's effect
pairs.mechanism: CYP2D6 makes a minor active metabolite (hydromorphone from hydrocodone). Blocking it can reduce analgesia somewhat.
pairs.action: Monitor pain control.

pairs.risk: metoprolol levels rise: slower heart rate, lower blood pressure
pairs.mechanism: Metoprolol is cleared by CYP2D6; inhibitors raise its level 2- to 5-fold.
pairs.action: Check heart rate and blood pressure; lower the metoprolol dose or switch to a beta-blocker not cleared by CYP2D6 (atenolol, bisoprolol).

pairs.risk: levels rise: risk of fatal arrhythmia
pairs.mechanism: Pimozide and thioridazine prolong QT in a dose-related way; blocking their clearance raises the risk of fatal arrhythmia. The labels contraindicate these combinations.
pairs.action: Do not use together.

pairs.risk: levels rise: sedation, parkinsonism, QT prolongation
pairs.mechanism: These drugs are cleared by CYP2D6; the labels cap the dose with strong inhibitors.
pairs.action: Use the label's reduced maximum dose.

pairs.risk: levels rise
pairs.mechanism: These drugs are cleared by CYP2D6; their labels halve the dose with strong CYP2D6 inhibitors.
pairs.action: Use half the usual dose.

pairs.risk: tizanidine levels rise 10- to 33-fold: severe low blood pressure and sedation
pairs.mechanism: Tizanidine is cleared by CYP1A2. Ciprofloxacin raises its exposure about 10-fold and fluvoxamine about 33-fold. The tizanidine label contraindicates both.
pairs.action: Do not use together.

pairs.risk: clozapine levels rise 2- to 5-fold: seizures, sedation, low blood pressure
pairs.mechanism: Clozapine is cleared mainly by CYP1A2. Fluvoxamine raises clozapine levels 3- to 5-fold and ciprofloxacin about 2-fold. The label advises a one-third dose with strong CYP1A2 inhibitors.
pairs.action: Reduce clozapine to one-third of the dose, check a clozapine level, and watch for sedation, seizures, and ileus.

pairs.risk: theophylline levels rise: seizures and arrhythmias
pairs.mechanism: Theophylline is cleared by CYP1A2 and has a narrow margin. Ciprofloxacin raises levels 20 to 100% or more, and fluvoxamine even more; toxicity causes seizures and arrhythmias.
pairs.action: Avoid, or cut the theophylline dose and check a level within 2 to 3 days.

pairs.risk: levels rise
pairs.mechanism: These drugs are cleared by CYP1A2; strong inhibitors raise their levels.
pairs.action: Use a lower dose and watch for side effects.

pairs.risk: citalopram levels rise: dose-related QT prolongation
pairs.mechanism: Citalopram is cleared by CYP2C19 and prolongs QT in a dose-related way. The citalopram label caps the dose at 20 mg a day with CYP2C19 inhibitors.
pairs.action: Keep citalopram at 20 mg a day or less, or switch to an antidepressant that does not prolong QT.

pairs.risk: clopidogrel may not work as well
pairs.mechanism: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19. Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19 and cut the active metabolite (efficacy loss); the clopidogrel label says to avoid them. The clinical harm is contested: the COGENT trial found no increase in cardiac events.
pairs.action: Use pantoprazole or famotidine if stomach protection is needed.

pairs.risk: contraceptive failure: unintended pregnancy
pairs.mechanism: These drugs induce CYP3A4 and speed the clearance of ethinyl estradiol and progestins, so hormonal contraception can fail (efficacy loss).
pairs.action: Use a non-hormonal or IUD method during the course and for 28 days after the inducer stops.

pairs.risk: HIV drug levels fall: treatment failure and resistance
pairs.mechanism: Strong inducers drop protease inhibitor and cobicistat levels, leading to virologic failure and resistance (efficacy loss). The labels contraindicate these combinations.
pairs.action: Do not use together.

pairs.risk: opioid levels fall: withdrawal or loss of pain control
pairs.mechanism: Rifampin, carbamazepine, and phenytoin induce CYP3A4 and cut opioid levels within days (efficacy loss), causing withdrawal; stopping the inducer later can cause overdose.
pairs.action: Raise the opioid dose under close monitoring, and lower it again when the inducer stops.

pairs.risk: statin levels fall
pairs.mechanism: CYP3A4 induction lowers statin exposure, so cholesterol lowering weakens (efficacy loss).
pairs.action: Check the lipid panel; use a higher dose or a statin not cleared by CYP3A4.

pairs.risk: quetiapine levels fall
pairs.mechanism: Phenytoin raised quetiapine clearance about 5-fold (efficacy loss); the label says the dose may need to rise up to 5 times.
pairs.action: Raise the quetiapine dose as needed, and lower it within 1 to 2 weeks after the inducer stops.

pairs.risk: lamotrigine levels fall about 40%
pairs.mechanism: These drugs induce lamotrigine's glucuronidation and cut its levels by about 40 to 50%.
pairs.action: Use the label's higher lamotrigine dosing with inducers, and re-adjust if the inducer stops.

pairs.risk: benzodiazepine levels fall
pairs.mechanism: Enzyme inducers speed benzodiazepine clearance; carbamazepine lowers clonazepam about 20 to 30%.
pairs.action: Usually minor; adjust if symptoms return.

pairs.risk: lamotrigine levels double: risk of serious rash (Stevens-Johnson)
pairs.mechanism: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine's glucuronidation and roughly doubles its half-life, raising the risk of serious rash including Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
pairs.action: Use the lamotrigine label's valproate dosing (about half the usual dose, slower titration) and teach the patient to report any rash.

pairs.risk: high ammonia with confusion (hyperammonemic encephalopathy) and low body temperature
pairs.mechanism: Both labels warn that the combination can raise ammonia and cause encephalopathy and hypothermia, even when valproate levels are normal.
pairs.action: Check ammonia if the patient becomes lethargic, confused, or vomits; stop one drug if it is high.

pairs.risk: valproate levels drop 60 to 100% within a day: breakthrough seizures
pairs.mechanism: Carbapenems block the enzyme that recycles valproate glucuronide, so valproate levels crash within 24 hours (efficacy loss), and extra valproate does not restore them.
pairs.action: Avoid; choose a non-carbapenem antibiotic or add another antiseizure drug for the course.

pairs.risk: free valproate rises and bleeding risk adds up
pairs.mechanism: Aspirin displaces valproate from albumin and slows its metabolism, raising free valproate; valproate can lower platelets, and aspirin blocks them.
pairs.action: Watch for bruising and valproate side effects; check platelets.

pairs.risk: valproate levels fall; carbamazepine epoxide rises
pairs.mechanism: These drugs induce valproate metabolism and lower its levels, and valproate raises carbamazepine's toxic 10,11-epoxide metabolite.
pairs.action: Check drug levels when either is started or changed, and watch for dizziness, double vision, and unsteadiness.

pairs.risk: blocks levodopa and worsens parkinsonism
pairs.mechanism: These drugs block dopamine D2 receptors, directly opposing levodopa and worsening Parkinson's symptoms. Metoclopramide's label warns against use in Parkinson's disease.
pairs.action: Avoid; for nausea use domperidone where available or ondansetron, and if an antipsychotic is needed use quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin.

pairs.risk: the antibiotic is not absorbed and may fail
pairs.mechanism: Calcium, iron, magnesium, aluminum, and zinc bind (chelate) the antibiotic in the gut; ciprofloxacin absorption falls by about 40 to 50%.
pairs.action: Separate the doses: give the antibiotic at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after the mineral product, or pause the supplement during the course.

pairs.risk: less levothyroxine is absorbed
pairs.mechanism: Calcium, iron, and binders hold levothyroxine in the gut and reduce its absorption.
pairs.action: Separate the doses by at least 4 hours and recheck TSH in 6 to 8 weeks.

pairs.risk: absorption may fall slightly
pairs.mechanism: Stomach acid helps levothyroxine and non-heme iron dissolve; acid suppression modestly reduces absorption.
pairs.action: Usually minor; recheck TSH or iron studies if control changes.

pairs.risk: less mycophenolate is absorbed (exposure falls 25 to 35%)
pairs.mechanism: Mycophenolate mofetil needs stomach acid to dissolve; with acid suppression less is absorbed, and exposure to the active drug (mycophenolic acid) falls 25 to 35%.
pairs.action: Monitor for rejection or consider enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium.

pairs.risk: slower stomach emptying changes oral drug absorption
pairs.mechanism: GLP-1 agonists slow stomach emptying and can change the timing and amount of oral drug absorption.
pairs.action: Usually minor; monitor glucose, INR, or TSH after starting.

pairs.risk: steroid builds up: Cushing's syndrome and adrenal suppression
pairs.mechanism: Ritonavir and cobicistat block CYP3A4 clearance of fluticasone and budesonide, so even nasal or inhaled doses reach systemic levels and cause Cushing's syndrome and adrenal suppression. The fluticasone label advises against the combination.
pairs.action: Switch to beclomethasone, or stop the nasal or inhaled steroid.

pairs.risk: PDE5 inhibitor levels rise up to 10-fold: low blood pressure
pairs.mechanism: Ritonavir raises sildenafil exposure about 11-fold; the sildenafil label limits the dose to 25 mg in 48 hours with ritonavir-class inhibitors.
pairs.action: Use sildenafil 25 mg no more than once in 48 hours (tadalafil 10 mg in 72 hours).

pairs.risk: severe, refractory low blood pressure
pairs.mechanism: Nitrates release nitric oxide, which raises cGMP; PDE5 inhibitors block cGMP breakdown (riociguat stimulates its production). Together blood pressure can fall sharply and not respond to treatment. The labels contraindicate these combinations.
pairs.action: Do not use together. Allow 24 hours after sildenafil or vardenafil and 48 hours after tadalafil before any nitrate.

pairs.risk: severe low blood pressure
pairs.mechanism: Riociguat raises cGMP and PDE5 inhibitors stop its breakdown; the riociguat label contraindicates PDE5 inhibitors.
pairs.action: Do not use together.

pairs.risk: symptomatic low blood pressure on standing
pairs.mechanism: Alpha-1 blockers and PDE5 inhibitors both widen blood vessels. The sildenafil label advises being on a stable alpha-blocker dose first and starting at the lowest PDE5 dose.
pairs.action: Start the PDE5 inhibitor at the lowest dose and separate the doses in time.

pairs.risk: rizatriptan levels rise about 70%
pairs.mechanism: Propranolol inhibits the MAO-A metabolism of rizatriptan and raises its levels about 70%.
pairs.action: Use rizatriptan 5 mg per dose, at most 15 mg a day, as the label directs.

pairs.risk: additive blood vessel constriction
pairs.mechanism: Triptans and ergots both constrict blood vessels; the labels contraindicate use within 24 hours of each other.
pairs.action: Do not use within 24 hours of each other.

pairs.risk: may reduce tramadol's pain relief
pairs.mechanism: Part of tramadol's analgesia runs through serotonin; blocking 5-HT3 receptors may reduce it (loss of effect).
pairs.action: Usually minor; assess pain control.

pairs.risk: risk of metabolic or lactic acidosis
pairs.mechanism: Topiramate and other carbonic anhydrase inhibitors cause a metabolic acidosis that adds to metformin's rare lactic acidosis risk; the topiramate label warns about this.
pairs.action: Check a bicarbonate level; stop metformin if acidosis develops or kidney function falls.

pairs.risk: topiramate exposure rises; potassium may fall
pairs.mechanism: Hydrochlorothiazide raised topiramate exposure about 30%, and both can lower potassium.
pairs.action: Check potassium if symptoms suggest it.

pairs.risk: calcium channel blocker levels rise: low blood pressure, swelling
pairs.mechanism: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are cleared by CYP3A4; strong inhibitors raise their levels modestly.
pairs.action: Monitor blood pressure and ankle swelling.

pairs.risk: tenofovir exposure rises; creatinine rises
pairs.mechanism: Boosters raise tenofovir disoproxil exposure, adding kidney risk, and cobicistat blocks tubular creatinine secretion (MATE1), raising creatinine without a true loss of filtration.
pairs.action: Monitor creatinine, urine protein, and phosphate; consider tenofovir alafenamide.

pairs.risk: additive, sometimes permanent hearing loss
pairs.mechanism: Aminoglycosides and loop diuretics both damage the inner ear; together hearing loss can be permanent. Aminoglycoside labels carry a boxed warning against potent diuretics.
pairs.action: Avoid if possible; monitor aminoglycoside levels, kidney function, and hearing.

pairs.risk: macrolide levels rise: about 5 times the rate of sudden cardiac death
pairs.mechanism: Erythromycin prolongs QT and is cleared by CYP3A4. With a CYP3A4 inhibitor its level rises; users of both had about 5 times the rate of sudden cardiac death (Ray et al., NEJM 2004).
pairs.action: Avoid; choose azithromycin or a non-macrolide antibiotic.

pairs.risk: tendinitis and tendon rupture
pairs.mechanism: Fluoroquinolones injure tendon tissue; the risk is highest with corticosteroids and after age 60. Fluoroquinolone labels carry a boxed warning.
pairs.action: Choose another antibiotic if possible; tell the patient to stop and call at the first sign of tendon pain.

pairs.risk: opposing effects partly cancel
pairs.mechanism: A stimulant works against sedating drugs and dopamine blockers; each may blunt the other.
pairs.action: Review whether both are needed.

duplicate_classes.risk: duplicate therapy, no added benefit, more serotonin syndrome and bleeding risk
duplicate_classes.action: Keep one antidepressant; cross-taper if switching (fluoxetine's long half-life needs a washout).

duplicate_classes.risk: duplicate therapy: next-day impairment, complex sleep behaviors, falls, slowed breathing
duplicate_classes.action: Keep one sleep medicine at the lowest dose.

duplicate_classes.risk: duplicate therapy: the total opioid dose (MME) adds up
duplicate_classes.action: Use one opioid, and count the total MME across all of them.

duplicate_classes.risk: duplicate therapy: more stomach bleeding, kidney, and heart risk with no added benefit
duplicate therapy: more movement side effects, QT, prolactin, and metabolic effects
duplicate_classes.action: Use one antipsychotic unless a psychiatrist is deliberately combining them.

duplicate_classes.risk: duplicate therapy: two dopamine blockers add movement side effects, tardive dyskinesia, and NMS risk
duplicate_classes.action: Avoid combining metoclopramide with an antipsychotic.

duplicate_classes.risk: duplicate therapy: two triptans must not be used within 24 hours of each other
duplicate therapy: low blood pressure, slow heart rate, sedation, and rebound hypertension if stopped
duplicate therapy: two ADHD medicines raise heart rate and blood pressure
duplicate_classes.action: Confirm the combination is intended and monitor heart rate and blood pressure.

duplicate_classes.risk: dual RAAS blockade: high potassium, low blood pressure, kidney injury
duplicate_classes.action: Use one ACE inhibitor or ARB.
Confirm this is a deliberate bridge; otherwise stop one.

duplicate_classes.risk: duplicate therapy: sedation and slowed breathing
duplicate therapy: more anticholinergic, QT, and overdose risk

acetaminophen.note: FDA labeling: no more than 4,000 mg a day from all sources

ketorolac.risk: bleeding and kidney injury; limit to 5 days

amphetamine.risk: raised heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia, misuse
amphetamine.note: mixed amphetamine salts for ADHD (up to 60 mg for narcolepsy)

lisdexamfetamine.risk: raised heart rate and blood pressure

methylphenidate.risk: raised heart rate and blood pressure

paroxetine.note: 60 mg for OCD and panic; 50 mg for depression

alprazolam.note: panic disorder maximum; 4 mg for anxiety

zolpidem.risk: next-day impairment and complex sleep behaviors
zolpidem.note: 5 mg for women and older adults

tizanidine.risk: low blood pressure and liver injury

simvastatin.note: 80 mg only for patients already on it for 12 months

lisinopril.risk: low blood pressure and kidney injury
